text:
Verses 26-48

This is the third set of verses following those at the commencement of this chapter, wherein the idolators mocked the Book and the Prophet and proposed to him a miracle other than the Qur’an. In this section, God, the Exalted, mentions the initial creation of humans and the jinn. He recounts His command to the angels and Iblīs to prostrate to Adam, their compliance, and Iblīs’s refusal, being of the jinn, leading to his expulsion. It also

describes Iblīs’s vow to mislead the descendants of Adam. These verses conclude by addressing God’s decree regarding the felicity of the righteous and the wretchedness of those who go astray.

(15:26) Certainly We created man out of a dry clay (drawn) from an aging mud,

al-Rāghib states in his al-M ufradāt: “The primary meaning of ṣalṣāl is the echoing sound produced by a dry object. Hence, we have the phrase ṣal al-mismār (echo of a nail). Dry clay is termed ṣalṣāl. The Almighty says: ‘He created man out of dry clay, like the potter’s’ (al-Raḥmān:14) and ‘Certainly We created man out of a dry clay (drawn) from an aging mud.’ The term ṣalṣālah refers to the residue of water. It is named as such due to the echoing sound it makes when moved within a container. Some also opine that ṣalṣāl refers to the foul odor emanating from clay, drawing a parallel with the phrase ṣalla al-laḥm (the meat decayed).”

He elaborates on the term ḥamʾah as well, saying, “It denotes foulsmelling black clay. As for the phrase, ‘from an aging mud,’ some interpret

it as undergoing a transformation. The term lam yatasannahu implies that it hasn’t changed, with the particle ‘ha’ indicating a state of rest.” This verse sheds light on the initial stages of human creation. Evidence lies in the verse: “He commenced man’s creation from clay. Then He made his progeny from an extract of a base fuid” (al-Sajdah:7-8). This verse delineates the creation of the human species and their emergence on Earth. The

creation of the very frst human mirrors the creation of subsequent ones. M ankind’s entirety originated from the frst, suggesting that all humans share a common mode of creation.

The author of Majma’ al-bayyān al-bayān elucidates: “The foundational substance from which Adam was formed was from the soil, as evident from the verse: ‘He created him from dust’ (Āl ʿImrān:59). This dust

was then transformed into clay, corroborated by the verse: ‘You created him from clay’ (al-A’rāf:12). This clay was then allowed to change until it became limp, as referred to in the verse: ‘W e created man out of a dry clay (drawn) from an aging mud.’ Eventually, this mixture was left until it desiccated, which is indicated by the phrase, ‘W e created man out of a dry clay.’ Hence, it is evident that these descriptions do not contradict but rather represent diferent phases of human creation.”

(15:27) and We created the jinn earlier, out of a piercing fre.

al-Rāghib states: “al-samūm is a hot wind that has a poisonous efect.” The root of the word jinn is to hide or cover. This meaning extends to all the derivatives of the word, including jinn, majannah (shield), jannah (paradise), janīn (fetus), janān (with the opening meaning heart), janna ʿalayhi al-layl (the night enveloped him), and others.

The jinn are a hidden group of beings by nature, not visible to our senses. They have feelings and free will. The Noble Qur’an frequently mentions them and attributes to them wondrous deeds and swift movements, as seen in the story of Solomon. They have obligations, they live,

die, and will be resurrected. Numerous scattered verses in the words of the Almighty indicate all of this.

As for the term jānn, the question arises: does it refer specifcally to the jinn? Or does it refer to the father of the jinn, much like Adam is the father of humans? Some reports suggest it could be Iblīs himself, as per Imām al-Ḥasan’s narration. Or perhaps jānn refers to the progeny of Iblīs among the jinn. Or maybe it’s a specifc kind of jinn as mentioned by al-Rāghib. These are various opinions with little conclusive evidence for most. W hat seems clear from contemplating the Qur’anic verses is that God is contrasting two distinct species in these verses: He juxtaposes insān (human) with jānn, presenting them as two distinct species with no intrinsic connection in their creation. This interpretation is also refected in the verse: “He created man out of dry clay, like the potter’s, and created the jinn out of a fame of fre” (al-Raḥmān:14-15).

Contextually, the verses under scrutiny clearly suggest that Iblīs belonged to the jinn. Otherwise, the mention of the statement: “and We created the jinn earlier, out of a piercing fre” would be meaningless. In another passage, God distinctly states about Iblīs: “He was one of the jinn, so he transgressed against his Lord’s command” (al-Kahf:50). Hence, the term jān in this verse either denotes the jinn as a whole or a specifc category within the jinn. This is the sole instance in the Qur’an where this term appears. Everywhere else, the term jinn is employed, even in contexts that encompass both Iblīs and his counterparts. For instance, God proclaims: “the devils from among humans and jinn” (al-Anʿām:112). Another verse goes: “And the word became due against them, as it did against the nations that passed away before them of jinn and humans” (Fussilat:25). There’s also the verse: “O company of jinn and humans! If you can pass through the confnes of the heavens and the earth, then do pass through it. But you will not pass through except by an authority” (al-Raḥmān:33).

The apparent juxtaposition between humans (insān) and the jān in some verses and between humans and jinn in others indicates that the terms jinn and jān refer to the same entity. This is evident.

W hen comparing the verse, “Indeed, We created man from a dry clay, (drawn) from an aging mud,” to the verse, “And We created the jinn earlier, from a piercing fre,” it becomes clear that the latter verse discusses the

original creation of the jinn and their emergence as a distinct species. This is analogous to the creation of humans from dry clay. A question arises: Is the subsequent creation of the jinn lineage similar to the creation of the frst jinn, specifcally, from a piercing fre? This contrasts with human creation where the frst human was formed from earth, while subsequent generations came from his sperm. The Qur’an does not explicitly mention this. Yet, it does refer to the progeny of Iblīs in the verse: “W ill you

then take him and his ofspring for guardians in My stead?” (al-Kahf:50). Another verse associates mortality with both humans and jinn: “And the word became due against them, as it did against the nations that passed away before them of jinn and humans” (Fussilat:25). It’s commonly understood that any species which has ofspring and experiences death reproduces. A subsequent question is: Do the jinn reproduce similarly to humans through copulation, or do they have a diferent reproductive method?

The phrase in the verse, “And W e created the jinn earlier,” is an annexation construction. However, its relation isn’t specifed. The comprehensive

interpretation of this verse is that the jinn were created before mankind. This understanding stems from the context comparing the two species.1 The verse states that the jinn were initially created from a piercing fame. This doesn’t confict with the verse which says: “and created the jinn out of a fame of fre” (al-Raḥmān:15). A fame of fre here denotes a fame accompanied by smoke. Combining insights from these two verses, it’s inferred that the jinn’s creation began with a piercing fame that ignited, becoming a smokeless fame of fre.

Consequently, the essence of these two verses (15:26-27) is: “By oath, We commenced the creation of the human species from a dry clay, which previously was a malodorous liquid. We initiated the creation of the jinn species from a piercing fame that ignited and transformed into a fame of fre.”

(15:28) When your Lord said to the angels, ‘Indeed I am going to create a human out of a dry clay (drawn) from an aging mud.’

al-Rāghib states: “The term bashrah (epidermis) means the outer layer of the skin, while admah denotes what lies beneath it. The majority of linguists opine that humanity is termed bashar because their skin

is exposed and not enveloped by hair, setting them apart from other animals whose skins are veiled by wool, fur, or fuf. Interestingly, both the

singular and plural forms of the word bashar (human) are identical. This term is employed in the Qur’an as seen in: ‘Shall we believe two humans

1 Editor’s note: In terms of interpretation, this means that although the direct grammatical construction doesn’t specify the exact nature of the temporal relationship, the surrounding context allows for a comprehensive understanding—thus, the conclusion that jinn were created before humans is derived from the overall comparison of the two entities within the Qur’anic narrative.

like ourselves?’ (al-M u’minūn:47). Notably, every instance in the Qur’an that touches upon human appearance utilizes the word bashar. An example being: ‘It is He who created the human being (bashar) from water’

(al-Furqān:54).”

The passage commencing with, “W hen your Lord said to the angels,”

has an implicit verb, making the complete meaning: “Remember when your Lord said to the angels….” This verse intriguingly transitions from the personal plural to the third person. This is analogous to our earlier discussion on the verse: “and indeed, it is your Lord who will resurrect them,” (15:25) where the verse addresses those who harbor doubts about resurrection. This verse also sheds light on the Day of Resurrection, eternal felicity, and perpetual distress.

The utilization of the frst-person plural in preceding verses like “We created man” and “We created the jinn” is emblematic of majesty. This style of speech is frequently observed among the nobility when they speak of themselves, their aides, and their subordinates, symbolizing their elevated stature. In this context, God views the noble angels as mediums executing His commands in these matters. Yet, they don’t assist Him in the act

of creating Adam. This is evident as they are the recipients of the message, learning about God’s will to create Adam and subsequently being

instructed to prostrate before him after He shapes him and breathes His spirit into him. The essence of the verse is self-evident.

(15:29) So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down in prostration before him.’

The term taṣwīyah refers to the act of making something stable and well-proportioned, ensuring that each part is in its appropriate place and condition. Likewise, when speaking of the human body, taṣwīyah implies the precise arrangement of limbs and organs in their appropriate positions and states.

The words: “Indeed I am going to create a human out of a dry clay (drawn) from an aging mud. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of M y spirit, then fall down in prostration before him,” possibly refer to the gradual formation of the frst human body. Initially, the act of creation (khalq) assembled the various parts of the human being. Then came the act of proportioning (taṣwīyah), which involved placing each part in its suitable place and condition. Lastly, the act of breathing (nafkh) of the spirit into the human occurred. This interpretation does not confict with the verse “He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be’, and he was” (Āl ʿImrān:59). The phrase, “then said to him, ‘Be’, and he was,” pertains to the creation of the human spirit or soul, not the physical body. This idea aligns with another Qur’anic verse which, after describing the gradual creation of the human body, states: Then We produced him as (yet) another creature (al-M u’minūn:14).1

The term nafkh generally means the act of blowing air into a body, either through the mouth or some other means. In the context of these verses, it metaphorically represents the divine act of originating the human spirit and linking it to the body. The spirit isn’t literally inside the body like air blown into a vessel. This concept is further elaborated in the verses: “Then We made him a drop of (seminal) fuid (lodged) in a secure abode. Then We created the drop of fuid as a clinging mass. Then We created the clinging mass as a feshy tissue. Then We created the feshy tissue as bones. Then We clothed the bones with fesh. Then We produced him as (yet) another creature” (al-M u’minūn:13-14). Another relevant verse is: “Say, ‘You will be taken away by the angel of death, who has been charged with you. Then you will be brought back to your Lord’” (al-Sajdah:11).

The frst set of verses illustrates that the human spirit is essentially connected to the body but without any addition to it. The second set indicates

that although the spirit leaves the body at the time of death, nothing is physically removed from the body.

Therefore, the spirit exists independently but has a form of attachment to the body. This connection ceases upon death, and the spirit is separated from the body. We have touched upon these concepts in our commentary on the verse: “And do not call those who were slain in Allah’s way ‘dead’” (al-Baqarah:154), in the frst volume of this book. We plan to further explore this topic in our forthcoming commentary on “Say, ‘The Spirit is of the command of my Lord’” (Al-Isrā’:85),2 God willing.

1 Editor’s note: This verse also implies that the beginning of the soul or spirit was the body itself.

2 See Eng. vol. 25. (Ed.)

In the verse (under discussion), God bestows honor upon the spirit by referring to it as M y spirit. This form of annexation not only serves as a means of honoring the spirit but also emphasizes God’s ownership of it. The phrase in the verse, “then fall down in prostration before him,” explicitly directs the angels to prostrate to Adam. It’s plausible to interpret this part of the verse as meaning “fall down upon the ground in prostration before him.” If this interpretation holds, it highlights the importance for the angels to exhibit humility towards this new creation.

The comprehensive meaning of the verse thus becomes: “Once I have properly proportioned him, completed the creation of his physical body, and brought into being the noble spirit—associated with Myself—and attached it to his body, then fall upon the ground in prostration before him!”

(15:30-31) Thereat the angels prostrated, all of them together, but not Iblīs: he refused to be among those who prostrated.

The terms ’ajma’ūn (all of them) and kulluhum are both used for emphasis, with the latter intensifying the former. This conveys that all the angels, without exception, prostrated before Adam. The sole exception was Iblīs. However, he wasn’t considered among the angels, as corroborated by the verse: “He was one of the jinn so he transgressed against

his Lord’s command” (al-Kahf:50). Some commentators have proposed an unlikely interpretation that a subset of angels were termed as jinn, and Iblīs was among this group. Others have mistakenly interpreted “jinn” in this context to mean “covered creation,” encompassing both angels and other beings. Such interpretations are not plausible. As we’ve previously explained in our commentary on Sūrah al-Ā’rāf, Iblīs was commanded to prostrate before Adam, even though he wasn’t one of the angels. The meaning of these verses is clear.

(15:32) He said, ‘O Iblīs! What kept you from being among those who have prostrated?’

The phrase, mā laka (what kept you)1 in the verse integrates both a subject and a predicate, translating to “what is that with you?” In this verse, the phrase allā takūn (from being) exemplifes the omission of the jussive particle (naz’ al-khāfz). This phrase essentially asks, “W hy weren’t you among those who prostrated?” Clearly, those who prostrated refer to the angels. Thus, the essence of this verse is: “What held you back from joining those who prostrated?”

(15:33) Said he, ‘I will not prostrate before a human whom You have created out of a dry clay (drawn) from an aging mud.’

In the phrase “I was not to prostrate,” (lam akun li-asjuda ) as opposed to saying “I will not prostrate” (lā asjudu) or “I am not prostrating (lastu asjudu),” there is an implication that his refusal to prostrate is intrinsic to his nature.2 It is as if it was expected of him if one were to truly understand his essence. This verse indirectly conveys what is explicitly stated in another verse, “I am better than him: You created me from fre, and You created him from clay” (al-A’rāf:12).

We’ve previously examined the implications of prostrating before Adam, God’s directive to the angels and Iblīs, the compliance of the angels, and the defance of Iblīs. For further insight, one can refer to our tafsīr of

Sūrah al-Baqarah and Sūrah al-A’rāf.3

1 Editor’s note: In Arabic, this phrase serves as an interrogative expression that

literally means “what is for you?” or “what is that with you?.” Here, “mā” is an interrogative particle that asks about the nature or identity of something, and “laka” is a prepositional phrase, where “la-” means “for” and “-ka” is a possessive pronoun meaning “you.” So, the phrase “mā laka” is integrated as both subject and predicate, encapsulating the idea of asking about something that concerns or belongs to you.

2 Editor’s note: Both phrases could be used to indicate a refusal to prostrate, but

they carry slightly diferent nuances. Lā asjudu is a straightforward expression of refusal, whereas lastu asjudu suggests a more inherent or characteristic refusal, as if to say prostrating is not something that one does by nature.

3 Eng. volumes 1 & 15 respectively. (Ed.)

(15:34-35) He said, ‘Begone hence, for you are indeed an outcast, and indeed the curse shall lie on you until the Day of

Retribution.’

The term rajīm (outcast) follows the fa’īl pattern, signifying something that has been acted upon. Rajm means to drive away, and it has commonly been used in the context of driving someone away using stones and pebbles. The term la’n (curse) signifes driving someone away from mercy.

From this, it becomes apparent that His statement, “and indeed the curse shall lie on you until the Day of Retribution,” serves as an elucidation for His previous statement, “you are indeed an outcast.” The act of rajm (driving away) led to his expulsion from the midst of the angels in the heavens or from a divine position.1 In essence, he was driven away from a station of closeness, a level of God’s unique mercy. This implies being distanced from God’s mercy, which the act of la’n (cursing) embodies. In another passage of the Qur’an, the Glorious attributes this curse imposed on Iblīs to Himself: “And indeed My curse will be on you till the Day of Retribution,” (Ṣād:78). In both verses, the duration of the curse is specifcally mentioned to last “until the Day of Judgment.”

The general imposition of the curse on him in the statement “the curse shall lie on you” is because every act of disobedience is linked to Iblīs. There is no act of disobedience wherein Iblīs doesn’t play a part, either by temptation or by whispering. He is the root cause of every sin, and every curse that accompanies these sins, even directly afecting the individuals who commit these sins, traces back to him. This recalls what has been mentioned in relation to another verse, “So that Allah may separate the bad ones from the good, and place the bad on one another, and pile them up together, and cast them into hell. It is they who are the losers,” (al-Anfal:37). Sending a la’n (curse), when done by anyone other than God, essentially acts as a du’ā (supplication) wishing for someone to be removed

from God’s mercy. In essence, the one who enacts this distancing from His mercy is God Himself. Therefore, this is an emphatic way to express

1 Editor’s note: Before the command to prostrate before Adam, Iblīs and the angels were in the station of sanctity with no distinction. However, they later split: the angels continued in humble servitude and obedience to God as depicted in the Qur’an, while Iblīs deviated from this path, separating himself from the angels.

the denial of mercy.

The author of Majma’ al-bayyān comments, “Some Qur’anic exegetes have observed that the word la’nah (cursing) is mentioned with the defnite article in the phrase ‘indeed the curse shall lie on you.’ Yet, in another verse from Sūrah Sād, it is phrased as ‘My curse’ in a possessive form. This is due to its preceding phrase, ‘to what I created with My own Hands.’ Since the phrase ‘My own Hands’ is possessive, ‘My Curse’ in this verse follows suit. Earlier, it was said: ‘O Iblīs! W hat prevented you from being among the sājidīn (those who prostrate)?’ This verse uses the defnitive form for the word sājidīn. The defnitive form is also used for the word insān (man) in ‘We created man’ and for jinn in ‘We created the jinn.’” The author concludes that this verse clarifes that Iblīs was never a believer.

The verse highlights that the act of la’nah (cursing) is limited until the Day of Retribution. This limitation implies that the curse stems from the self-inficted spiritual harm and maladies due to one’s transgressions before God. The opportunity for such wrongdoings concludes with the Day of Retribution, signaling the end of this world of action, in contrast to the hereafter, a realm of recompense. In essence, this life is where deeds are noted, and the Day of Retribution is the time for accountability and just compensation.

Several Qur’anic commentators interpret the limited duration of the curse until the Day of Retribution as evidence of its cessation on that day. The verse’s apparent meaning suggests that retribution will transpire on that particular day. This interpretation is reinforced by the reference to the Day of Judgement as the Day of Retribution in this verse, implying Iblīs’s curse lasts until then, followed by his punishment. If the retribution were to end prior to this day, it would be referred to as the “Day When Retribution Ceased,” rather than the Day of Retribution.

To address the ambiguity surrounding the ultimate end, some suggest that it represents the furthest limit set by the creation. This is analogous to the verse: “They shall remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure” (Hūd:107). As you can observe, you have already understood its meaning, as discussed in the exegesis of Sūrah Hūd.1

1 Editor’s note: In the exegesis of Ch. 11, verse 107, the author says: “God links

the permanence of Heaven and Hell and their inhabitants to the persistence of the heavens and earth because the heavens and earth, in their general sense One could contend that the curse alluded to in the verse pertains to the curse of creation, set to end with the Day of Judgment. However, this stands in contrast to the eternal nature of the Divine curse and God’s act of distancing someone from His Mercy. This perspective seemingly overlooks the verse from Sūrah Ṣād, which states, “And indeed M y curse will

be on you till the Day of Retribution” (Ṣād:78).

(15:36) He said, ‘My Lord! Respite me till the day they will be resurrected.’

The term indhār signifes granting a respite. Iblīs initiated his conversation with God using the address, my Lord, as he was making a supplication. Despite his concurrent arrogance, defance, and disobedience

towards God, he was compelled to address God in a manner invoking His boundless mercy due to his supplicatory stance. He sought God, invoking His dominion over him, hoping for His response, even in his defance. Iblīs’s plea to God starts with the particle fā, which leads the sentence “Respite me.” This indicates his intent to target all humans, not just Adam. As noted in our exegesis of verses in Sūrah al-Ā’rāf, Iblīs was directed to prostrate to all humans, with Adam merely symbolizing them as the focal point for this act. This is evident from the verse: “Certainly W e created you, then W e formed you, then W e said to the angels, ‘Prostrate before Adam.’ So they (all) prostrated, but not Iblīs” (al-A’rāf:11). The angels were instructed to prostrate to humanity at large, not just the individual, Adam.1 This prostration was not just a symbolic act; it had a profound purpose. It was a gesture of the angels’ inherent humility towards humans, refecting (in that they will be transformed into a new heavens and a new earth in the hereafter), are eternal and not transient. However, these heavens and earth that we experience in this world will come to an end based on the observable order. As for the heavens that shade Heaven, for instance, and the earth that carries it, which are illuminated by the light of their Lord, they are permanent and never fading. The universe will never be devoid of them” (Eng. vol. 21).

1 Editor’s note: Adam was setup as the qiblah (direction) for their prostration much like the Ka’bah which is set as a direction in worship and is symbolic to facing God. Adam was presented to the angels on behalf of all humans. that angels, by their nature, are in service to humans. This underlines the elevated nature of humans. Essentially, angels aid humans, channeling blessings into their lives due to the unique merit and higher accomplishments humans possess, which even surpass those of angels.

The act of angels prostrating to mankind signifes their subservience in aiding human success. Indeed, they serve as agents paving the way for human prosperity. Such angels encompass those responsible for life, the harbingers of death, the bestowers of sustenance, the conveyors of revelation, those that accompany humans, the guardians, the recorders, and

numerous others detailed in the Qur’an. Consequently, angels act as a guiding medium, assisting humans in their pursuit of perfection and accomplishment.

Upon refecting on these verses, it becomes evident that Iblīs’s refusal to prostrate to Adam stemmed from his aversion to humble himself to humanity and to aid in their journey toward success and perfection. He chose not to embrace the role that angels had accepted. Thus, by declining to prostrate to Adam, he distanced himself from the company of the

angels. This sentiment is echoed in the verse: “He said, ‘O Iblīs! W hat prevented you from being among those who prostrated?’” (15:32). Furthermore,

he expressed his intent to oppose humans for the entirety of their earthly existence.

The evidence of God’s disdain towards him is manifested in the imposition of an unbounded curse upon him, spanning from his act of defance to

the Day of Judgment. This duration aligns with the tenure of humanity on earth, ensuring the curse remains efective throughout this time frame. This imposition predates Iblīs’s declaration of his intent to lead humans astray, as stated: “I will mislead them all, every one of them” (15:39). It suggests that his refusal to prostrate was born out of deep-seated animosity towards the human race, starting with Adam and extending to his last descendant. Seemingly, the accursed one discerned from God’s pronouncement:

“The curse shall lie on you till the day of Retribution” (15:35), a linkage between his fate and that of humanity until the Day of Resurrection. Their tribulations and moral degradation are tied to his initial act of disobedience in not prostrating. This realization perhaps led him to plead for a delay in his doom until the resurrection of mankind. He implored: “My Lord! Respite me till the day they will be resurrected” (15:36). Notably, he didn’t seek respite limited to Adam’s lifespan but extended his plea to encompass Adam’s progeny until their collective resurrection. This plea aligns with the continuation of the curse till the Day of Resurrection. Once granted, his concealed intentions emerged, as he proclaimed: “I will mislead them all, every one of them” (15:39).

(15:37-38) He said, ‘You are among those who are reprieved until the Day whose time is known.’

God’s response to Iblīs is revealing. In it, we observe that a portion of Iblīs’s plea is accepted, while another portion is declined. The part that is granted pertains to the respite in lifespan he sought. However, the declined segment pertains to the stipulation that the respite be extended “until the Day they are resurrected.” Reviewing the context of these verses, it becomes apparent that the Day with a predetermined time (the Day whose time is known) difers from the “Day they are raised again.” It wasn’t allowed for Iblīs to receive reprieve until the Day they rise again; instead, it was a different day. Undoubtedly, this day precedes the day humans are resurrected.

From this, the faw in the argument of those who assert that these two days in the verses are identical becomes evident. An example supporting this is God’s statement: He said, “You are one of the reprieved” (al-A’rāf:15), which doesn’t impose any restrictions.

The claim that the two days in these verses are the same is refuted by what’s previously discussed. The argument citing the unbounded nature of the verse from Sūrah al-Ā’rāfiis invalidated because it’s limited by what is said in this sūrah and in Sūrah Ṣād, especially the phrase: “until the Day whose time is known” (15:37, 38:81). This manner of stipulation is frequent in the Qur’an, where some sections attest to others, and some elucidate others. The evident interpretation of the “Day whose time is known” is that it’s a predetermined moment within God’s knowledge. This resonates with His declaration: “W e only send it down in a known measure” (15:21). In the same vein, His statement: “For such there is a known provision,” (al-Ṣāfāt:41) mirrors this sentiment. Therefore, this time is undeniably known to God. Whether Iblīs is aware or unaware of it remains unclear based on the verse’s phrasing. Some argue that God purposely kept the specifcs of this day ambiguous, not elucidating it. Hence, while it is discernible to God, it remains a mystery to Iblīs. They posit that had this day been explicitly revealed to Iblīs, it might tempt him into further misdeeds. However, this notion lacks concrete evidence. Just because we fnd the phrasing ambiguous doesn’t imply Iblīs did too. And to suggest that revealing the day would

spur Iblīs to commit further wrongs—given he’s the origin of all evil—is speculative at best. Take heed of this!

Furthermore, Iblīs’s declaration, “I will mislead them all, every one of them,” (15:39) stands as evidence that he will endure until the last human, susceptible to his deceit, exists in this world. Iblīs inferred from God’s statement, “until the Day whose time is known,” (15:37) that it denotes the fnal day of humankind on earth, where he can continue his attempts to lead them astray.

Ibn ‘Abbās is attributed with the view, widely accepted by the majority, that “the day” alludes to the fnal day of divine accountability, coinciding with the initial trumpet’s blow when all beings will perish. This perspective seems anchored in the belief that Iblīs will persist as long as divine accountability exists, along with the potential for defance and disobedience, mirroring humanity’s lifespan on earth. This era concludes with the inaugural

trumpet’s sound, marking the end for all life. This moment represents the “Day whose time is known,” for which God has granted Iblīs a respite. Separating the frst trumpet from the next— heralding resurrection— is a span of either four hundred or forty years, as per difering narrations. This diference underscores the contrast between Iblīs’s appeal and God’s decree. referred to as “doors,” just as one would say “categories of sustenance” (abwāb al-rizq), “categories of evil” (abwāb al-sharr), and “categories of mercy” (abwāb al-rahman). God states, “We opened for them the gates of all (good) things” (al-An’ām:44). Sometimes the means to something or the ways to reach it are termed as ‘doors’, like the “pathways to sustenance” due to various types of earnings and dealings.

It’s plausible to derive the second meaning from various verses about Hell, such as His words: “The faithless will be driven to Hell in throngs. W hen they reach it, and its gates are opened…” (al-Zumar:71), and “Indeed the hypocrites will be in the lowest reach of the Fire” (al-Nisā’:145), among other verses.

Supporting this is His saying, “and to each gate belongs a separate portion.” The apparent meaning suggests that the specifed class (juz’) is allocated to a gate (bāb), which is more consistent with the interpretation of

a gate as a category (ṭabaqah) rather than an entrance (madkhal). Some interpret the assigned portion (or allotted share, juz’ muqasūm) as a distinct group or sect (frīq mu’ayyin) separated from others, which seems evident. Based on this, the fact that Hell has seven gates indicates that the punishment prepared within it varies into seven categories. Each category then divides according to the division of the group that enters and resides within. This implies that the sins leading to entry into Hell are divided into seven categories, as well as the paths leading to and reasons prompting those sins. This supports the traditions conveyed about these meanings, as will be elaborated upon, God willing.

(15:45-46) Indeed the Godwary will be amid Gardens and Springs: ‘Enter it in peace and safety!’

M eaning, they are settled in gardens and springs. It will be said to them: “Enter it in peace,” a description that cannot be detailed nor is its attribute withheld, signifying that you are safe from all harm and evil.

When God mentioned His decree concerning those who followed Iblīs from among the misled, He also stated His decision for the righteous, which is Paradise. The description of Godwary (or piety, taqwā)

is found in the Messenger’s words as avoiding what is forbidden by God. Repeatedly, the Qur’an has conveyed the glad tidings of Paradise to the pious (muttaqūn), implying that the pious encompass more than just the devoted.

Some argue that the context of these verses unmistakably suggests that the pious are the same individuals previously described as those who have achieved sincerity. They also maintain that generic terms are wholly applicable to all their individual members.

This perspective stems from the interpretation that the “servants”

mentioned in the verse: “Indeed as for My servants, You do not have any authority over them” (15:42), refer exclusively to those rendered sincere, so much so that they confne the scope of this statement solely to this group. However, we have highlighted that “servants” encompasses all of humanity, with only the misguided being the exception. God has clearly stated that the misguided will be destined for the Fire. In contrast, this verse underscores that Paradise is the ordained abode for everyone other than the misguided. The fate of those incapable of accountability and those committing grave sins remains unaddressed. Regarding those who perpetrate severe sins and pass away unrepentant, their ultimate fate hinges on potential intercession.1 Hence, the ones left are the pious among the believers, a category broader than those deemed sincere. Their decreed fate is entry into Paradise. Concerning the notion that an absolute term should be applied to a ‘complete individual,’ this is a mistaken view. Instead, the term should refer to an ‘individual’ as commonly understood. A more detailed discussion on

In his exegesis, Imām al-Rāzī notes that the term al-M uttaqīn (the Godwary or pious) in the verse refers to those who abstain from polytheism (shirk). He attributes this interpretation to a consensus among the majority of the Companions and the Successors, citing their views as evidence.

He elaborates further:

“This is indeed the correct and valid understanding. What supports this claim is that the term al-M uttaqī refers to someone

who has exercised taqwā even just once, similar to how al-Ḍārib (one who strikes) refers to someone who has struck even just once. Thus, it is not necessary for the description to be accurate that one must embody all facets of taqwā. Supporting this view is the fact that one who fulflls even a single aspect of taqwā is considered to have taqwā, as fulflling any individual aspect inherently encapsulates the essence of taqwā. Therefore, anyone who

demonstrates taqwā should rightfully be termed Muttaqī. This is why some have said: ‘The apparent meaning of an imperative does not require repetition.’

The apparent reading of the verse suggests that anyone who refrains from even a single sin is entitled to gardens and springs in the hereafter. However, there is a unanimous consensus within the community that this entitlement is conditional upon abstaining from disbelief.

Furthermore, this verse appears after Iblīs’s statement: “Except Your exclusive servants among them,” which follows God’s proclamation: “Indeed as for My servants, You do not have any authority

over them.” Consequently, faith is a critical factor in this ruling. Therefore, it’s essential that no additional conditions should be imposed, as limiting the general rule should be minimized to align more closely with the original and apparent meaning of the text.

Therefore, it is confrmed that the ruling in question applies universally to all who declare: “There is no god but God, Muḥammad

is the Messenger of God,” even if they belong to the ranks of the sinful. This is an unequivocal afrmation, and the message is plain to see.”

The essence of his argument suggests that the verse includes anyone who abstains from shirk, even if they engage in all the major sins that lead to Hellfre according to the Noble Qur’an, or neglect all obligatory duties that, when neglected, also warrant the same punishment. However, anyone deeply engrossed in refecting upon the Divine verses will fnd it incontrovertible that such an individual is not termed Muṭṭaqī by the Qur’an nor

counted among the Muṭṭaqīn. Indeed, the Qur’an frequently refers to the M uṭṭaqīn, explicitly promising them Paradise in nearly twenty instances, and often describes them as those who steer clear of prohibitions. Thus, taqwā is defned in the narrations in this same vein, as we have mentioned. Indeed, simply meeting the conditions to be described by a particular term is diferent from actually being labeled with that term. One is not called a “believer,” “doer of good,” “obedient,” “sincere,” or “patient,” especially when these descriptors imply an ongoing state, unless these characteristics are frmly rooted in them. If al-Rāzī’s claim about the M uṭṭaqīn

holds true, then the same reasoning would also apply to categories such as the wrongdoers, immoral, corrupt, criminals, misguided, and the lost— all of whom God has warned with Hellfre. This would result in a puzzling inconsistency and imbalance in the divine text. If one argues that some verses could shift the meaning of these labels to cover isolated or occasional acts— just like the verses concerning repentance and intercession— then other verses could similarly shift the scope of this specifc verse to cover a Muṭṭaqī who commits a sinful act once or twice. Examples include the verses warning against major sins such as fornication, unjust killing, usury, and misappropriating the wealth of orphans, and other similar verses. Subsequently, al-Rāzī provides various unfounded justifcations to elucidate his explanation, referencing the sequence of statements by Iblīs and God. Given our previous discussions, it’s evident that this argument holds no weight. He further contends that introducing an additional condition to this verse beyond faith contradicts its primary meaning. However,

the primary meaning is referenced only in the absence of linguistic cues. As you’re well aware, numerous Qur’anic verses ofer clear constraints on this matter.

Regarding his statement that this contradicts the apparent meaning (of the verse), it appears he’s alluding to the clear meaning of a statement when taken at face value. Yet, he seems to have missed the fact that

the straightforward understanding of an unqualifed statement stands as evidence only when there’s no valid explanation that can specify its scope.1 In reality, the verse only encompasses those in whom the quality of Taqwā has taken root—that is, abstaining from acts that God has forbidden. These individuals are the ones assured of eternal happiness and

Paradise. Furthermore, what is gleaned from both the Qur’ān and the Sunnah is that people professing Tawḥīd—those who afrm that there is no god but God—will not remain in Hell forever and are guaranteed entry into Paradise. This is distinct from what the verse concerning the term M uṭṭaqīn suggests.

(15:47-48) We will remove whatever rancor there is in their breasts–brothers, (reclining) on couches facing one another.

Therein neither weariness shall touch them, nor will they (ever)

be expelled from it.

The term “resentment” (al-ghill) refers to grudges or ill-will. Some say it encompasses both grudges and envy that may drive a person to harm others. The term “couches” (al-surur) is the plural of “couch” (sarīr), and “hardship” (al-naṣb) refers to the physical and emotional difculties that come from external factors.

The verses describe specifc blessings among the multitude of blessings in Paradise to underline certain points. They emphasize that the residents of Paradise are in a state of peace and security, free from the trials that those who have gone astray have to face—such as the loss of happiness, sovereignty, and dignity. God tells us that they are safe even from themselves

since He has removed any resentment (or rancor) from their hearts. They sit as “brothers, (reclining) on couches facing one another,” and the signifcance of their sitting arrangement (facing one another) will be covered in

later narrational discussions, God willing.

An Excursus

The decrees that were issued from the Source of Dignity at the outset of human creation, according to His statements— Exalted is He— are ten: (1) The frst and second are in His words to Iblīs: “Get out from here, you are indeed accursed. The curse will be on you till the Day of Reckoning”

(15:35). These two can be considered as one.

(2) The third is in His words: “You are among those who are reprieved until the Day whose time is known” (15:38).

(3) The fourth, ffth, and sixth are His words: “You have no authority over any of M y servants except for the misled who follow you ” (15:43). (4) The seventh and eighth are His words to Adam and those with him: “Go down from here as enemies to each other! You will have residence on the earth and enjoyment for a time” (al-Baqarah:36).

(5) The ninth and tenth are His words to them: “Go down from it, every one of you! Then when guidance comes to you from M e, those who follow My guidance will feel no fear and will know no sorrow. But those who

disbelieve and deny Our Signs are the Companions of the Fire remaining in it tim elessly, for ever” (al-Baqarah:38-39).

There are also subsidiary decrees that follow these foundational ones, which can be discovered by the thoughtful researcher.

Examining Narrations

(1) In the exegesis of Tafsīr al-Ayyāshī, it is reported from M uḥammad b. M uslim, who narrates from Imām al-Bāqir, “I asked him about the verse from the Qur’an: ‘And I breathed into him of M y spirit.’ He said: This is a spirit that God created, and He breathed it into Ādam.”

(2) Additionally, Abū Baṣīr narrates from Imām al-Sādiq regarding the verse, ‘So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of M y spirit,’ the Imām said: “He created a form and created a spirit, then commanded the angel to breathe it into the form.

This spirit is not something that diminishes anything from God;

it is from His power, exalted is He.”

Author’s comment: Both narrations emphasize that the spirit breathed into Ādam is a creation of God and is not something that takes away from His essence or attributes. It is an act of His divine power.

(3) In another narration in Tafsīr al-Ayyāshī, as well as in the account from Samāʿah, it is related from the Imām al-Sādiq: “Ādam was created and the spirit was breathed into him. W hen I asked him about the spirit, he said: ‘It is His (God’s) power from the celestial realm .’” Author’s comment: This means that it is His active power, emanating from His essential power, as evidenced by the preceding report.

(4) In Ma’ānī al-Akhbār, it is narrated through its chain of transmission from Muḥammad b. Muslim, who said, “I asked Imām

al-Bāqir about the verse of God, the Mighty and Majestic, ‘And I breathed into him of M y spirit.’ He said: ‘It is a spirit that God chose, favored, created, and attributed to Himself, and preferred it over all other spirits. Then He commanded that it be breathed into Ādam.’”

(5) In al-Kāfī, through its chain of transmission, Muḥammad b.

M uslim said: “I asked Imām al-Bāqir about what is narrated that God created Ādam in His own image. He replied: ‘It is in the image of a created, originated form that God chose and preferred over all other difering forms. He attributed it to Himself, just as He attributed the Kaʿbah to Himself, saying, “My House” and “And I breathed into him of M y spirit.”’

Author’s comment: These narrations are among the most enlightening on the nature of the spirit (rūh) and include profound insights. We will clarify their meanings when discussing the reality of the spirit, God willing. (6) In Tafsīr al-Burhān, it is reported from Ibn Bābūyah through his chain of narrators from Imām al-Ṣādiq regarding the verse, “Indeed, you are of those reprieved until a known Day.” He said, “On the day when the trumpet will be blown once, Iblīs will die between the frst and second blowing.”

(7) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Wahb b. Jumayʿ, and in Tafsīr al-Burhān, from Sharafial-Dīn al-Najafī, omitting the chain of transmission from Wahb, the wording attributed to the latter from Imām al-Ṣādiq who said: “I asked him about Iblīs and the verse, ‘M y Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected,’ and God’s reply ‘Indeed, you are of those reprieved until a

known Day.’ Which day is it? He replied, ‘O Wahb, do you think it is the day on which God will resurrect people? Rather, God has reprieved him until the day when our Qāʾim will rise. He will then seize him by his forelock and strike of his head. That day is the known time.’”

(8) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, it is narrated through its chain from Muḥammad b. Yūnus from a man who heard from Imām al-Ṣādiq concerning the verse, “Indeed, you are of those reprieved until a known Day,” he said: “The known Day is when the Messenger of God will slaughter him on the rock that is in Jerusalem.”

Author’s comment: These reports pertain to the concept of Rajʿah (the return) and carry similar meanings to the preceding narrations. There are other reports about this from the path of the Ahl al-Bayt.

It is possible that the frst narration among the last three could have been issued in the context of Taqqiyah (dissimulation). The three narrations can be reconciled without contradiction, in light of what was previously discussed on the topic of Raj’ah in the frst part of the book. It is

worth noting that the narrations from the path of the Ahl al-Bayt often interpret most of the verses related to the Resurrection as referring at times to the appearance of al-Mahdī, at times to the Raj’ah, and at other times to the Resurrection. These three days share the unveiling of truths but difer in intensity. The rule that applies to one of them extends to the others. Understand this.

(9) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Jābir from Imām al-Bāqir, who said: “I asked, ‘What is your explanation` of God’s statement, “Indeed, as for My servants you do not have any authority over them”? He replied, ‘God means you have no power to make them enter either Paradise or Hell.’”

(10) In Tafsīr al-Qummī regarding the verse, “It has seven gates,” one of the infallibles replied:“Each gate is for the followers of a certain school of thought, and Paradise has eight gates.”

Author’s Comment: The various accounts elaborate on the structure and purpose of the gates of Hell. These are not to be understood as mere physical gates but should be comprehended at a metaphysical level. The discourse is not limited and should not be understood as exhaustive. (11) In al-Durr al-manthūr, it is cited from Aḥmad’s Kitāb al-Zuhd, narrating from Khattāb b. ʿAbdullāh, who said that Imām ʿAlī described: “Do you know how the gates of Hell are? We said, ‘Like these doors?’ He said, ‘No, but they are like this,’ and he placed one hand over the other and spread one hand upon the other.”

(12) Also, it cites Ibn al-Mubārak, Hunād, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd b. Ḥumayd, Aḥmad in his book on Asceticism, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in the Description of Hell, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in the Resurrection, narrating from Imām ʿAlī: “The gates of Hell are seven, some above others. The frst will be flled, then the second, then the third, until all are flled.”

(13) Further, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khaṭīb in his Tārīkh Baghdād narrate from Anas, who said that the Messenger of God said concerning the verse, “and to each gate belongs a separate portion of

them,” that “One portion (of people) associated partners with God, another doubted God, and another was heedless of God.”

Author’s Comment: This narration enumerates the components of the gates rather than the gates themselves. From the context, it’s clear that they are not limited only to these three.

(14) Finally, in the same source, it cites Ibn M ardawayh narrating from Abū Dharr, who said the Messenger of God stated: “There is a gate in Hell through which none shall enter except those who betrayed me concerning my family and shed their blood after me.”

Author’s comment: The word “betrayed” (khafarahu) implies deceit and the breaking of covenants.

The traditions below delve into various aspects of the afterlife, particularly Paradise and Hell, as well as the deep spiritual connection among the

Ahl al-Bayt and their followers. It is worth noting that the insights provided in these accounts are consistent with what we have previously discussed. (15) In al-Durr al-manthūr, it is cited from Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, alTabari, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in “The Resurrection,”

narrating from ʿUtba b. ʿAbdullāh who reported from the Prophet as saying: “Paradise has eight gates and Hell has seven, and some are greater than others.”

Author’s comment: The traditions, as you can see, substantiate what we have put forth earlier.

(16) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, regarding the verse, “And We will remove whatever rancor there is in their breasts,” one of the infallibles stated that this refers to enmity.

(17) In Tafsīr al-Burhān, narrated from al-Hafz Abu Naʿim through his chain of narrators from Abū Huraira, ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib is reported to have asked the Messenger of God: “Who is more dear to you, me or Fāṭimah?” The Prophet replied: “Fāṭimah is dearer to me than you, but you are more honored to me than her. I foresee you at my pool (Hawḍ), defending it against people. You will have pitchers as numerous as the stars, and you, al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥusayn, Ḥamzah, and Jaʿfar will be brothers in Paradise, reclining on elevated couches, and you will be with me along with your

followers.” Then the Messenger of God recited the verse, “(They are) brothers, (reclining) on couches facing one another.” No one will look into the faults of another.

(18) From Ibn al-Maghāzilī in M anāqib Ahl al-bayt, raising it to Zayd b. Arqam, it is reported: “I entered upon the Messenger of God, who said, ‘I create brotherhood among you as God created brotherhood among the angels.’ Then he said to ʿAlī, ‘You are my brother,’ and recited the verse, ‘(They are) brothers, (reclining)

on couches facing one another.’ The friends for the sake of God will look at each other.”

Author’s Comment: This account is also narrated from Aḥmad in his Musnad, attributed to Zayd b. Awfā from the Prophet, and the narration is extensive.

In these accounts, the interpretation of God’s statement, “(They are) brothers, (reclining) on couches facing one another” is elucidated in two ways: One is that no one will look into the faults of another, and the other is that friends for the sake of God will look at each other. These interpretations hint at the idea that the ‘facing one another’ in the verse symbolizes

the absence of tracking each other’s faults and mistakes, something that people with resentment in their hearts would do. It is a subtle yet meaningful interpretation.

The Prophet’s recitation of the verse (15:47) is merely from the perspective of fow and applicability, not that the verse was revealed specifcally

about the Ahl al-Bayt. The context of the verses does not ft this notion at all.

Similar accounts include narrations from ʿAlī stating that the verse was revealed about the people of Badr. In another narration from him, it is said to have been revealed about Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. A diferent narration from ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn (peace be upon them) says it was revealed

about Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿAlī. Other accounts attribute the revelation to various combinations of the early companions, including ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, and others, as well as one narration from Ibn ʿAbbās stating that it was revealed concerning ten individuals including Abū Bakr,

ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, Saʿīd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf, and ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd.

Despite the variations in these narrations, they are applications (of the verse) by the narrators, not explicit explanations of the verse’s revelation. The context of this verse, within a series of verses describing God’s decrees and judgments from the time of Adam’s creation, involving the angels and Iblīs, strongly suggests that the verse was not revealed specifcally about any of the aforementioned individuals.
